title: An army against emus and a concert on a roof

questions.question: Lake Burley Griffin is named after the American architect who designed Canberra, but he died in 1937 without ever seeing it. In which decade was the lake finally filled?
questions.explanation: Scrivener Dam was closed in 1963, the lake filled in 1964 and Robert Menzies opened it that October. Griffin's original plan dates from 1912.
questions.source: National Capital Authority

questions.question: Western Australia's entire land border follows a single line of longitude, the 129th meridian east. Which two jurisdictions lie on the other side of it?
questions.answer: The Northern Territory and South Australia
questions.explanation: At about 1,860 kilometres it is one of the longest straight borders in the world. Surveying errors mean the two halves do not quite meet at Surveyor Generals Corner.
questions.source: Geoscience Australia; Landgate WA

questions.question: Prime Minister Harold Holt disappeared while swimming on 17 December 1967. Off which Victorian beach, near Portsea, was he last seen?
questions.explanation: His body was never found. Melbourne later named a municipal swimming pool after him, in Glen Iris, in the electorate he had represented.
questions.source: National Archives of Australia; National Museum of Australia

questions.question: The Australian $50 note carries the inventor and writer David Unaipon on one side. Which woman, the first elected to an Australian parliament, is on the other?
questions.explanation: Cowan won the seat of West Perth in the Western Australian Legislative Assembly in 1921. The note also shows the original Parliament House in Perth.
questions.source: Reserve Bank of Australia

questions.question: In which South Australian opal-mining town do many residents live in underground homes known as dugouts, to escape the summer heat?
questions.explanation: The town also has underground churches and hotels. Its name is usually said to come from Aboriginal words meaning, roughly, white man's hole.
questions.source: District Council of Coober Pedy; South Australian Tourism Commission

questions.question: In late 1932, soldiers armed with Lewis machine guns were sent to cull emus that were destroying wheat crops, an episode now called the Emu War. In which state did it take place?
questions.explanation: The operation, around Campion in the wheatbelt, was led by Major G. P. W. Meredith. The emus scattered too quickly to be hit in numbers and the army withdrew within weeks.
questions.source: National Museum of Australia; National Archives of Australia

questions.question: Four of the five stars in the Southern Cross on the Australian flag have seven points. How many points does the fifth and smallest star, Epsilon Crucis, have?
questions.explanation: The large Commonwealth Star beneath the Union Jack also has seven points: one for each of the six states and one for the territories.
questions.source: Department of the Prime Minister and Cabinet, Australian National Flag

questions.question: On 1 July 1983 the High Court ruled that the Commonwealth could stop a hydro-electric dam being built in the Tasmanian wilderness. Which river did the decision save?
questions.explanation: The dam was to be built on the Gordon River, below its junction with the Franklin. The blockade that preceded the case saw more than 1,200 people arrested.
questions.source: High Court of Australia, Commonwealth v Tasmania (1983); National Museum of Australia

questions.question: The Indian Pacific crosses the Nullarbor on the longest dead-straight stretch of railway in the world. Is it closest to 280, 480 or 680 kilometres long?
questions.explanation: The straight runs for 478 kilometres between Ooldea in South Australia and Loongana in Western Australia without a single curve.
questions.source: Guinness World Records; Journey Beyond Rail

questions.question: An Australian town is hiding inside this sentence, its letters in order and unbroken across the words: "The global ban yielded few results." Which town is it?
questions.explanation: It runs from the end of global through ban to the start of yielded. Albany, on the south coast of Western Australia, was the last Australian port many Anzac troops saw in 1914.
questions.source: Checked by inspection; City of Albany

questions.question: Thanks to islands scattered either side of both the equator and the 180th meridian, which Pacific nation is the only country in the world to sit in all four hemispheres?
questions.explanation: Its 33 islands are spread over an area of ocean about as wide as the continental United States. The name is pronounced Kiribas.
questions.source: CIA World Factbook; Government of Kiribati

questions.question: Istanbul is split between Europe and Asia by a narrow strait that links the Black Sea to the Sea of Marmara. What is the strait called?
questions.explanation: At its narrowest it is about 700 metres wide. A rail tunnel under the strait, the Marmaray, opened in 2013.
questions.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Bosporus

questions.question: The shortest war on record was fought on 27 August 1896 and was over in well under an hour. Britain's opponent was which island sultanate off the coast of East Africa?
questions.explanation: Most accounts put the fighting at between 38 and 45 minutes. It began when a new sultan took power without British approval.
questions.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Anglo-Zanzibar War

questions.question: Only two chemical elements are liquid at ordinary room temperature. Mercury is one. Which reddish-brown non-metal is the other?
questions.explanation: Its name comes from the Greek for stench. Caesium and gallium melt just above room temperature, close enough to turn liquid in a warm hand.
questions.source: Royal Society of Chemistry, Periodic Table

questions.question: On 12 April 1961 Yuri Gagarin became the first person in space, completing a single orbit of the Earth in 108 minutes. What was his spacecraft called?
questions.explanation: Gagarin did not land inside the capsule. He ejected at about seven kilometres and came down by parachute, a detail the Soviet Union kept quiet for years.
questions.source: NASA; European Space Agency

questions.question: Which African country uses a calendar of 13 months, which runs seven to eight years behind the calendar used in most of the world?
questions.explanation: Twelve months have 30 days each and the thirteenth has five, or six in a leap year. Ethiopia celebrated the start of its year 2000 in September 2007.
questions.source: Encyclopaedia Britannica, Ethiopian calendar

questions.question: The Rosetta Stone, which repeats one decree in three scripts and unlocked Egyptian hieroglyphs, was found by French soldiers in 1799. In which museum has it been displayed since 1802?
questions.explanation: The three scripts are hieroglyphic, demotic and ancient Greek. Jean-François Champollion announced his decipherment in 1822.
questions.source: The British Museum

questions.question: People with which blood type are known as universal donors, because their red blood cells can be given to almost any patient in an emergency?
questions.explanation: Fewer than one in ten Australians has it, which is why blood services so often appeal for O negative donors.
questions.source: Australian Red Cross Lifeblood

questions.question: A doubly landlocked country is one surrounded entirely by other landlocked countries. Only two exist, one in Europe and one in Central Asia. Name either.
questions.explanation: Liechtenstein sits between Switzerland and Austria. Uzbekistan is bordered by five countries, none of which has a coastline on the open sea.
questions.source: CIA World Factbook

questions.question: News that Edmund Hillary and Tenzing Norgay had reached the summit of Everest was held back so that it broke in London on the morning of which royal occasion in June 1953?
questions.answer: The coronation of Queen Elizabeth II
questions.explanation: They reached the top on 29 May. The Times correspondent James Morris sent the news in code to protect the scoop, and it was published on 2 June.
questions.source: Royal Geographical Society; The Times archive

questions.question: Don Bradman needed four runs in his final Test innings, at The Oval in 1948, to retire with an average of 100. Which English leg-spinner bowled him for a duck, second ball?
questions.explanation: Bradman finished on 99.94. Hollies took more wickets in his first-class career than he scored runs.
questions.source: ESPNcricinfo; Bradman Museum

questions.question: Which mare is the only horse to have won the Cox Plate four times, doing so in consecutive years from 2015 to 2018?
questions.explanation: She retired in 2019 on a run of 33 consecutive wins. Her first foal to reach the sale ring sold for $10 million in 2024.
questions.source: Moonee Valley Racing Club; Racing Australia

questions.question: Australia's strict animal quarantine laws meant the equestrian events of the 1956 Melbourne Olympics were held months earlier and half a world away. In which city?
questions.explanation: It is the only time events from one Olympic Games have been held on two continents. Stockholm had hosted the full Games in 1912.
questions.source: International Olympic Committee

questions.question: In 2010 the Federal Court found that the flute riff in Men at Work's Down Under reproduced part of which children's song, written in 1932 for a Girl Guides competition?
questions.answer: Kookaburra Sits in the Old Gum Tree
questions.explanation: The song was written by Marion Sinclair, a Melbourne teacher. The publisher that owned the rights was awarded five per cent of the song's royalties from 2002.
questions.source: Federal Court of Australia, Larrikin Music v EMI Songs (2010)

questions.question: Which is the only country to have played at every men's FIFA World Cup since the tournament began in 1930?
questions.explanation: Brazil has also won it more often than anyone else. Germany and Italy have each missed at least two tournaments.
questions.source: FIFA

questions.question: The Beatles' last public performance was an unannounced lunchtime concert in London on 30 January 1969, which police eventually asked them to turn down. Where did they play it?
questions.answer: On the roof of their Apple headquarters in Savile Row
questions.explanation: The set lasted about 42 minutes. It ends the film Let It Be and takes up much of the final part of Peter Jackson's Get Back.
questions.source: The Beatles, official site; British Film Institute

questions.question: Which Japanese director made Seven Samurai in 1954, the film Hollywood remade six years later as the western The Magnificent Seven?
questions.explanation: His Yojimbo was remade as A Fistful of Dollars, and George Lucas has said The Hidden Fortress helped shape Star Wars.
questions.source: British Film Institute; The Criterion Collection

questions.question: Peter Carey won his second Booker Prize in 2001 for a novel written as if in the unpunctuated voice of a bushranger. What is it called?
questions.answer: True History of the Kelly Gang
questions.explanation: Carey drew on the style of Ned Kelly's Jerilderie Letter. His first Booker was for Oscar and Lucinda in 1988.
questions.source: The Booker Prizes

questions.question: In the 1997 film The Castle, the Kerrigan family's holiday house is beside a lake in which real Victorian town, where Darryl admires the serenity?
questions.explanation: The town is on Lake Eildon, north-east of Melbourne. The film was shot in 11 days.
questions.source: National Film and Sound Archive of Australia

questions.question: Cate Blanchett won her first Academy Award for playing another Oscar-winning actress in Martin Scorsese's The Aviator. Whom did she play?
questions.explanation: It made Blanchett the first person to win an Oscar for portraying an Oscar winner. Hepburn herself won four, still the record for an actor.
questions.source: Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences
